meta.subtitle: Revenue growth held above 20% in the second quarter, but memory costs cut gross margin and the shares sit near their 52-week low

analystSentiment.commentary:
Calix's second quarter of 2026 was a growth quarter with a margin problem. Revenue for the three months ended June 27, 2026 rose {+ +21.3% +} year over year, led by appliances, while gross margin slipped on memory component costs the company itself names. The business is debt-free and generated cash in FY25.

The share price tells a harsher story than the filing. At $34.34 the stock sits just above its 52-week low of $32.35 and roughly half its 52-week high of $71.22. The 30 closes in the price history show the slide still running, with the shares drifting lower across the period to today's level. No captured source explains the fall. There is no earnings-call transcript and no headline in this report's sources, so we cannot say whether the market is reacting to guidance, to memory costs or to something else. We treat the unexplained decline as information in its own right and weight the Bear case heavily for it.

The valuation is reasonable on consensus estimates but not compelling once the risk of those estimates being cut is priced. Our call is HOLD, close to the BUY line; Valuation sets out the split that decides it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Calix sells platform, cloud and managed services to broadband service providers, which the 10-Q calls communications service providers (CSPs) that it aims to turn into communication experience providers (CXPs). The offer combines the Calix Agent Workforce, intelligent appliances, software, cloud and SmartLife managed services. Wi-Fi systems sell under the GigaSpire and GigaPro brands.

The company reports one segment but splits revenue into two lines: Appliance, and Software and service. Software is sold on a per-subscriber basis, so that line grows as customers add subscribers. Sales run through a direct sales force and select resellers, and almost all revenue comes from the United States.

The customer count differs by source. The 10-Q cites approximately 1,600 active customers, while the July 20, 2026 press release says "more than 1,200 customers" use the Calix One platform. The two likely measure different things; we use the 10-Q figure for the installed base. The fiscal year ends December 31, so the company's second quarter of 2026 is the three months ended June 27, 2026.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Calix is growing well and has no debt, but its margins are thin and under fresh pressure. Second-quarter 2026 revenue of $293.3M rose {+ +21% +} year over year, while gross margin fell on higher memory component costs (Financials). On consensus estimates the stock trades at ~14.9x FY27E EPS, which would be cheap if the estimates hold. The shares have roughly halved from their 52-week high without an explanation in any captured source, and that unexplained fall is the main reason we do not lean on those estimates. We rate the shares HOLD: the upside on Base is real, but the Bear case is too likely to make the reward/risk a BUY.

catalysts: Software and service gross margin recovering now that the dual-cloud period of the third-generation platform migration has passed (Financials).
Further quarters of appliance growth from new customers, which the company attributes to taking footprint from legacy box vendors (Growth).
Continued share repurchases funded from internal cash, with no borrowings to service (Management).
International revenue rebuilding as the company turns more attention abroad with its third-generation platform (Growth).
risks: Memory component prices, which the company says are rising because of the AI infrastructure build-out, could keep compressing appliance margins (Risks).
The share price fall is unexplained in this report's sources, so consensus estimates may not yet reflect whatever caused it (Valuation).
One customer passed the 10% revenue threshold in the second quarter, raising exposure to a single buyer's timing (Risks).
Revenue depends on service providers' capital spending and on government broadband programs, both of which can pause (Risks).

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue has been volatile across the five years. Year-over-year growth ran {+ +27.7% +} in FY22 and {+ +19.8% +} in FY23, fell {- -20.0% -} in FY24, then recovered {+ +20.3% +} in FY25. Gross margin rose each year from 49.9% in FY23 to 56.8% in FY25. Operating margin has not followed: it was 2.1% in FY25 after a loss-making FY24, and 5.5% over the trailing twelve months.

The second quarter of 2026 extended the growth. Appliance revenue rose 23% and Software and service revenue 16%, both year over year. The company credits appliance growth to new customers adopting its platform "as we continue to take footprint from legacy box vendors" and to expansion within existing customers. It credits Software and service growth to CXP customers adding subscribers. Operating margin reached 7.4% in the quarter, above the trailing figure.

Gross margin is the weak spot. It was 54.6% in the second quarter against 56.3% a year earlier, a decline of 170 basis points that the company attributes primarily to "increased component memory costs". Over the six months, Software and service gross margin fell 550 basis points, which the company ties to running a dual cloud environment while customers migrated from the second-generation to the third-generation platform. That cause should fade; the memory cost pressure may not.

FY25 diluted EPS was $0.26 on net income of $17.9M. Thin GAAP earnings are why the trailing multiples discussed in Valuation look high.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet carries no debt; the 10-Q shows no borrowings, so net debt is not a meaningful measure here. Total equity was 0.9 ($B) at the end of FY25.

The cash figures differ by source. The vendor's Cash & ST Investments line shows 0.1 ($B) for FY25, while the March 27, 2026 proxy statement cites "record cash and investments of $388 million" at the end of 2025. The proxy figure likely includes longer-dated investments the vendor line excludes; we use the proxy figure as the fuller measure of liquidity.

The current ratio has come down from 4.24 at the end of FY25. It remains comfortable, so liquidity is not a constraint on the thesis.

The balance-sheet risk sits in working capital rather than leverage. The company lists inventory valuation and supplier purchase commitments among its critical accounting estimates, and its risk factors warn that changing customer requirements may affect the value of both. With memory prices volatile, a write-down is the balance-sheet item to monitor.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation improved sharply in FY25. Free cash flow margin was 11.6%, up from 6.1% in FY24 and above every earlier year in the five-year series. The proxy statement describes FY25 free cash flow as a "record".

The series is uneven, and one strong year does not establish a new level. FY22's margin was close to zero, and the company's own filing stresses that quarterly results fluctuate with customer budget cycles and seasonal buying. The FCF yield on the current market value is moderate.

The company returned cash through buybacks in FY25 rather than dividends; it pays none. Free cash flow covered both capital expenditure and those repurchases, so the buyback did not draw on the balance sheet. Whether FY26 cash flow holds up depends on gross margin and on how much inventory the company buys ahead of memory price increases, which the risk factors flag.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The trailing multiples overstate how expensive the stock is. The P/E (TTM) of 45.8x and EV/EBITDA (TTM) of 25.0x rest on thin GAAP earnings; P/S of 1.9x is a better read on what the market pays for the revenue base.

The forward multiples rest on consensus EPS of $1.72 for FY26E and $2.30 for FY27E. The vendor's Fwd P/E (NTM) of 19.9x matches FY26E EPS at today's price, so it is a current-year multiple rather than a strict next-twelve-months one. On FY27E EPS the stock trades at ~14.9x.

Those estimates sit far above FY25 diluted EPS and above what the trailing P/E implies, so they are likely on an adjusted basis. The sources do not reconcile them to GAAP, and the forward multiples should not be read as GAAP-based.

The vendor peer set is not a set of broadband-equipment or software businesses, so this report makes no peer-multiple comparison.

The Street is far more bullish than this report. Six of seven analysts rate the stock Buy and one Hold, with a consensus target of $62.33 and targets ranging from $52.00 to $85.00. Even the lowest target sits well above the current price. The dates of those targets are not visible, so we cannot tell whether they reflect the fall in the share price.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: 12-month horizon. Consensus estimates hold or rise, memory costs ease and the shares re-rate to the Street median target of $60.00. Requires the market to pay well above today's multiple, not just delivery of the current consensus path.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: 12-month horizon. FY27E consensus EPS of $2.30 is delivered. Two readings are equally likely: the stock carries its 19.9x current-year multiple onto that EPS a year from now (about $46), or keeps only the ~14.9x it pays on FY27E today, which is today's price. Base is the midpoint, about $40.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: 12-month horizon. Earnings stall at FY26E consensus EPS of $1.72 and the shares pay only the FY27E multiple named in Base, about $25.60. Consistent with memory costs persisting, a pause at the large second-quarter customer, or a cut to estimates that explains the fall in the share price.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Base is a one-year roll. A year from now FY27E is the fiscal year in progress, so carrying today's current-year multiple onto FY27E EPS needs no expansion. That multiple, however, rests on the visible EPS step from FY26E to FY27E. The market could just as easily pay only the lower multiple it already pays on FY27E, which leaves the shares at today's level even with FY27E EPS delivered. On the roll side, second-quarter revenue growth ran ahead of the FY26E consensus pace. On the flat side, gross margin is falling on memory costs and the share price has halved without a stated cause. Neither side clearly wins, so Base sits at the midpoint and the target range runs from the flat reading to the full roll.

Bear gets 35%, a heavy weight, because the market may know something the filings here do not show; the price near its 52-week low is the evidence. Bull gets 15% because it needs a re-rating, not only delivered estimates. Base gets 50%.

The weighted fair value of $37.96 gives expected upside of {+ +10.5% +} against bear-case downside of {- -25.5% -}, a reward/risk of 0.41×. The page's rule derives HOLD: the upside clears the BUY threshold, but it does not cover the Bear downside by enough.

The call is close. A Bear weight nearer 30%, with the difference moved to Bull, would derive BUY; that split would say the price fall is mostly sentiment. Against it, the second quarter's margin decline is a real, company-stated cause for estimates to drift lower, and no source rules out a larger one. We think the heavier Bear weight is the honest one while the fall stays unexplained, so the HOLD rests on that split.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Calix reports a single segment covering FY25 revenue of $1B. Inside it, the 10-Q splits revenue into Appliance and Software and service; appliances are the larger line by a wide margin. Software and service carries the higher gross margin, which was 63.0% in the second quarter against 52.8% for Appliance. The economic case for the business is that appliances seed a per-subscriber software relationship. That shift is still early: Software and service grew more slowly than Appliance in the quarter, so the mix moved toward the lower-margin line.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs
moatFactors.body: Customers that run their subscriber engagement, operations and managed services on Calix Cloud and SmartLife build workflows around the platform, and per-subscriber software pricing ties revenue to the customer's own subscriber growth. The 10-Q does not disclose retention or churn, so the strength of this lock-in cannot be measured.

moatFactors.name: Customer breadth
moatFactors.body: An installed base in the low thousands of service providers, from small regional operators to large carriers, spreads demand. The breadth is partial: one customer exceeded 10% of revenue in the second quarter of 2026.

moatFactors.name: Cost position
moatFactors.body: Calix depends on third-party vendors and component markets, and its risk factors say component price volatility and shortages have affected, currently are affecting and may affect gross margin. It has no stated cost advantage over rivals that buy the same memory parts.

moatFactors.name: Returns
moatFactors.body: Operating margins have stayed in low single digits or below zero across FY23 to FY25. A moat should show up as durable excess returns, and the reported margins do not yet show them.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NONE. The platform may create switching costs as more customers adopt the software and managed services, but the financial record does not yet show the excess returns a moat should produce. The risk factors also describe "intense competition" and rapid technological change, which limit how long any product lead lasts. The rating would move to NARROW if Software and service grew faster than Appliance for several quarters while operating margin rose, since that would show the per-subscriber model taking hold.

points: Consensus expects FY26E revenue of ~$1.2B, a {+ +19% +} rise, and FY27E revenue of $1.4B. Second-quarter revenue growth ran slightly ahead of that pace. The risk is that a slower second half, which seasonal budget cycles and government programs can cause, would pull the year back toward or below it.

Appliance growth comes from new customers and from expansion at existing ones, by the company's account. Appliance growth is the bulk of the revenue gain, but it is also the line exposed to memory component costs, so faster appliance growth can lower the blended gross margin.

Software and service growth tracks CXP customers adding subscribers. This is the higher-margin line and the core of the long-term case, but it grew more slowly than appliances in the second quarter, so the mix did not improve.
Demand visibility improved in FY25: the proxy statement reports remaining performance obligations up 18% year over year. That figure is for the end of 2025 and predates the second quarter.

International revenue fell year over year in the second quarter. The company says its near-term focus remains the U.S. and Canada, where government stimulus is funding underserved areas, but plans to increase attention on international markets with its third-generation platform. We give that plan no weight until it shows up in revenue.

management.leadership: Michael Weening is president and chief executive officer and Cory Sindelar is chief financial officer, both named executive officers in the proxy statement dated March 27, 2026. John Durocher was appointed chief operating officer in November 2025, and Shane Eleniak is chief product officer. Carl Russo, a director since 1999, is chairman. The proxy describes 2025 as a year of "strong, disciplined execution", which the FY25 revenue recovery supports; the thin operating margin shows that execution has not yet reached profitability.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation favors reinvestment and buybacks. The company pays no dividend, carries no debt and repurchased shares in FY25 with free cash flow. It continues to invest in the third-generation platform, agentic AI and customer success. Buybacks at today's lower price buy more shares per dollar than they did near the 52-week high, but the filing excerpt does not say how much authorization remains, so we cannot size future repurchases. Executive pay is tilted to the share price: 2025 equity grants were 100% stock options, half service-based and half performance-based, which deliver value only if the stock rises.
management.governance: Governance comes from the proxy statement dated March 27, 2026. Seven of nine directors are independent under NYSE rules. The two who are not are Mr. Russo, the chairman, and Mr. Weening, the CEO. The chair is separate from the CEO but is not independent, and the excerpt does not show whether the board has a lead independent director. For 2025, base salaries were kept flat for the CEO and CFO, bonuses paid at 108% of target, and the previously uncapped non-GAAP gross margin bonus metric was capped at two times target bonus. The cap is a sensible fix for a metric that could otherwise reward margin over growth. Overall the structure is conventional and gives outside holders no specific concern.
management.insiderOwnership: Per the proxy's table as of March 17, 2026, Mr. Russo beneficially owned 10.16% of outstanding shares, a figure that counts options exercisable within 60 days. All current directors, director nominees and executive officers as a group held 17.44%, much of it in options. BlackRock reported 14.97%, based on a Schedule 13G/A filed July 18, 2025, so that stake is over a year old. No holder approaches control. Insider ownership is large enough to align management with outside holders but too small to block them.

idiosyncratic: Memory component costs. The company says memory prices are rising because of shortages caused by the large-scale build-out of AI infrastructure, and it named them as the main cause of the second-quarter gross margin decline. If Calix cannot pass the cost on, appliance margins fall further and consensus EPS comes down. The signal to track is appliance gross margin in the third quarter against the prior year.

Customer concentration. One customer accounted for 12% of revenue in the second quarter of 2026, although no customer passed that threshold over the six months or in the prior-year periods. The risk factors warn that losing a key customer, or delays in its payments, could hurt revenue, cash flow and working capital. The test is whether that customer's share holds or drops back below that line in coming quarters.

Unexplained share price fall. The stock trades just above its 52-week low after roughly halving from its high, and no captured source explains the move. If the cause is a guidance cut or a margin issue not yet in consensus, estimates fall and the Bear case becomes the base. The next quarterly report is an early chance to see whether estimates move.

Inventory and supplier commitments. Changing customer requirements may lower the value of inventory and supplier purchase commitments, per the risk factors. Buying memory ahead of price increases raises that exposure, so a write-down in cost of revenue is the item to watch.
risks.systemic: Calix depends on the capital spending of service providers, and the risk factors warn that any decrease or delay in that spending would reduce revenue. Government-sponsored broadband programs and U.S. federal government shutdowns can shift the timing of customer purchases, and the company says government stimulus is part of why it focuses on the U.S. and Canada. Trade policy is a second channel. In February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the broad IEEPA tariffs exceeded the administration's authority; the company says it saw no significant financial impact because the majority of its finished goods are exempt, but new duties could still affect costs and demand. First-quarter seasonality, when customers finalize annual budgets and winter limits fiber deployment, adds to quarter-to-quarter swings.

body: HOLD, target range $34–$46, resting on the Base case and weighting set out in Valuation.

We would move to BUY if the third quarter shows year-over-year gross margin growth and Software and service growth outpacing Appliance, or if a disclosed cause for the share price fall proves temporary. We would move to SELL on a year-over-year decline in quarterly revenue or a cut to FY27E consensus EPS.
